extracted.subtask_description: Overview guidance and descriptive standards for reporters and editors covering wartime or politically sensitive foreign news, explaining national censorship systems and practical practices for getting truthful dispatches out. Emphasizes impartiality, withholding militarily useful details, verification, timing, and use of neutral channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality of reporters
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece insists correspondents should be impartial despite pressures; warring nations may block hostile critics and advise or order them to leave, but impartial reporting is presented as a cornerstone of truthful dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish military information useful to the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all countries bar what they consider military information 'that might be useful to an enemy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censors typically restrict material on military matters; reporters must avoid publishing details (troop movements, timings, technical military data) that could assist an adversary while still seeking to convey essential facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform to local timing rules for sensitive events
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries (e.g., Germany) correspondents 'must conform to official reports on air raids, and send the news only after the raid is over.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of and obey host-country timing restrictions (e.g., delayed reporting of air raids), which are enforced even when other freedoms exist; plan dispatch timing accordingly while seeking corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid untruthful or damaging attacks on host governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must 'refrain from untruthful, damaging attacks on the Nazi government' (example given for Germany).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where 'censorship of responsibility' operates, journalists are expected to avoid knowingly false or libelous material and personal attacks that could be suppressed or used against them; maintain factual grounding to resist censorship challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use neutral-country channels to transmit dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents have unhampered telephone communication with neutral countries to transmit their dispatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct channels are restricted, use telephone or telegraph links via neutral countries (e.g., Switzerland) and bureaus abroad to move copy and to compare information with foreign offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assay official announcements against other sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Assay official announcements in the light of other accurate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AP recommends cross-checking and comparing official statements with foreign versions and other reliable sources so censorship or propaganda can be exposed and the essential facts brought out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit multiple international bureaus to overcome censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The AP organization 'spreads further than does censorship' and what isn't known in one country usually becomes public in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate between bureaus and use reports from other capitals to piece together censored stories; pooling information across borders helps reveal truths that local censors hide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know national/regime-specific censorship systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship systems vary by country (examples: Soviet Russia examines dispatches but generally allows critical matter abroad; Germany/Italy use 'censorship of responsibility'; Japan is most rigorous; Switzerland lightest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must understand the particular rules and practices of each country — what is permitted, what must be delayed or censored, and how to work within or around those constraints to report accurately and safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect restricted communications and adjust reporting strategy in occupied areas
rubrics_metrics.description: In occupied countries communications may be cut and facts hidden, but secrecy often arouses suspicion and occupation authorities may loosen regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting from or about occupied territories, anticipate information gaps, seek alternative sources (refugees, neutral correspondents), and probe persistent discrepancies to force loose or reveal facts over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and resourcefulness over passive obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship obeyed with fear and accepted passively would stifle intelligent reporting; 'there is nothing mysterious about getting truthful news' and 'intelligent reporters aren't passive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article urges reporters to be proactive — use verification, alternate channels, and inter-bureau cooperation rather than passively accepting official suppression — while respecting safety and legal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report essential facts even when details are censored
rubrics_metrics.description: Although exact details (times, extent of damage) may be suppressed, 'German versions and British comment quickly bring out essential facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on reporting the core, verifiable facts that can be established despite redactions; use contextual reporting and corroboration from other national accounts to present the essentials without endangering operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of censorship softening or tightening trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship regimes can loosen or tighten (e.g., Vichy France 'softened' its old war censorship; occupation authorities usually loosen regulations as the lesser evil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor changes in censorship practices over time; adapt sourcing and publication approaches when regimes shift their policies to maximize reporting opportunities while minimizing risk.
